## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Engineers at AI-native startups keeping an LLM agent working for customers in production.
   [LYC] "Before starting Lemma, we were engineers at two high growth, AI-native startups: Tandem (AI for healthcare) and
   Chipstack (AI agents for chip design)." [LYC] "If you're building with LLMs and run a ton of prompt or eval
   experiments, we'd love for you to work with us." → `roles[engineer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Keep the agent doing what customers need as real traffic changes.
   [LYC] "AI agents don't learn from their mistakes. In fact, they get worse with use." [LYC] "In production, prompts
   and agents continuously degrade due to real-world input drift (new user behaviors or unseen edge cases)."
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When the agent starts failing on real inputs nobody tested.
   [LYC] "Agent performance can often drop ~40% in a few weeks, and suddenly what worked in testing breaks in front of
   customers." [LYC] "When that happens, engineers are forced to dig through logs, collect failing examples, and manually
   tweak prompts rather than building core product features." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: agent failure`.
   Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; the launch says
   "continuously" and gives no count. The daily rhythm is confirmed only later, by a customer quote on [SITE]: "Every
   morning, I check our frontend logs -> backend logs -> Lemma logs, then pipe any issues straight into Claude".
   Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most") is the author's: not every team's agent fails every week.

4. **Which people.** Engineers at US pre-seed to Series A startups with an agent serving customers.
   [LYC] "If you know a Head of AI/Eng or CTO at a pre-seed to Series A startup, we owe you lunch :)" → `context.segment`,
   `market: US` (author's choice: the founders are in the US batch and name no other market).

5. **Who pays.** The startup; its CTO or head of AI decides.
   [LYC] the ask above names the buyer, no payer or terms. → `persona.decision_maker: {role: founder}` (label
   "Startup CTOs and founders"; the id reads "The founder decides" in the engine's sentence). Buyer and payer tests
   "Nobody else" (at pre-seed the technical founder buys tools alone), with "The CEO" and "The security lead" listed:
   author's choice. Purchase friction's three items (a security review of sending traces out — tested; a check against
   the current observability tool; access to open pull requests) are the author's, drawn from [LYC]'s mechanism
   ("automatically open a PR in your codebase") and [YCP]'s "the silent failures your observability tools and evals
   miss". Commitment's step "connect one agent's traces for a trial": [LYC] "book a live demo on our website"; [WB]
   "Book a demo appointment to get started."; the trial on one agent is the author's next step after the demo.

6. **Mechanism.** Failed runs found in live traffic; the cause traced; a prompt fix opened as a pull request.
   [LYC] "Step 1: Lemma detects failed outcomes directly from live traffic, and it automatically identifies the exact
   cause in an agent chain." "Step 2: Lemma alerts you, and with one click, it runs targeted prompt optimizations to fix
   the failing behavior without any manual tracing or guesswork." "Step 3: We give you back an improved prompt and
   automatically open a PR in your codebase so your prompts can live where you want them." [LYC] "Agent tracing
   observability with live drift detection, regression alerts, and performance visibility across real user
   interactions." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (every run already traced — tested;
   prompts in the repository; traces may leave the company) and Adoption friction (review and merge the prompt changes
   it opens — tested; add its tracing to the agent's code). Relative advantage: [LYC] "resolve production drifts in
   minutes instead of days" (easier_recovery) and "cut manual prompt iteration by 90%" (shorter_time); wording the
   author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price is public at launch or since; the cost is a rate of failing runs.
   [LYC] asks for demos and introductions and names no price; [WB] "Book a demo appointment to get started."; [PRC] 404.
   → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $300 to $600 per agent a month: **the operator's reading**, not a source. The
   unit is the cost's (a chain price follows the cost's unit and period); the amount is the author's, a sum a CTO can
   approve alone that sits well under one engineer-week ([BLS]). `statements.commercial` carries the same reading.
   Existing sacrifice, RATE 10% to 40% of the agent's runs in production per agent a month, lossPhrase "Runs that fail in
   front of customers before anyone notices": the top is [LYC]'s "~40%", read as a share of runs (the launch says
   "performance"); the low end is the author's. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent of runs never
   compares with dollars), so the six founders answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [LYC] "dig through logs, collect failing examples, and manually tweak prompts". [YCP] "We catch the silent failures
   your observability tools and evals miss (think bad tool calls, lost context, and infinite loops) before your users
   find them." (today's page, later than launch). [SITE] (customer, later) "almost immediately it flagged an issue that
   had gone unnoticed in prod for 20+ days".

- Omar Haddad → [P2] "many existing agent monitoring systems depend heavily on developers deciding beforehand what they want to measure. This can include configuring specific judges, traces, evaluation criteria, alerts or known failure conditions." — a team whose own judges catch the known failures (Current solution mostly works).
- Lucía Romero → [LYC] the manual prompt loop; [SITE]'s "Agents can look like they're working even when they've failed." (later).

Startup CTOs and founders (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Nathan Cole → [LYC] the ask to "a Head of AI/Eng or CTO at a pre-seed to Series A startup"; pays below the founder's band per agent (several small agents; the per-agent price adds up), though he would start the trial.
- Farah Siddiqui → author's invention: prices it below the band against the observability tool she already pays for, and wants a week on staging first (Commitment yes after trying).
- Wei Zhang → [SITE] (customer, later) "we switched over from raindrop a while back": a buyer who already pays for an observability tool and prices this below it.
- Isabel Duarte → [SITE] (customer, later) "it flagged an issue that had gone unnoticed in prod for 20+ days": a buyer who would pay above the band (beyond), with the CEO agreeing.
- Marcus Oyelaran → author's invention, filling a gap: a low-volume agent read by hand, so Nothing as the cost and would not pay.
- Chloe Bennett → [P2] agents "in workflows where failures have financial, operational or customer-facing consequences"; author's invention: a security lead who must clear any vendor seeing customer conversations, and a buyer who cannot say the cost or the price (both escapes).

The split (1 of the 5 founders who name a rung at $300 or above, the other four below it -- made harsher on
2026-10-22 so the price fails; 3 of 5 cost boxes at 10% or more) is the author's
reading of a crowded tooling market ([P2] "The emerging AI observability market includes tools for tracing model calls,
measuring latency, monitoring token usage, evaluating model responses and reviewing agent behavior.") against the
launch's claims. No respondent carries the name of a customer, commenter or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Same idea, re-led. The problem is unchanged (agents fail in production without anyone noticing); the lead product moved
from "Continuous Learning" and automated prompt optimization ([LYC], [WB]) to monitoring: [SITE] "Lemma | Production
monitoring for AI agents"; "Lemma audits every trace against your agent's instructions and groups recurring failures
into issues."; "Pull context into your coding agent to resolve it without context-switching." Raised $2.3 million
pre-seed ([P2], 2026-08-19). Price today: none public ([PRC] 404; [SITE] "Book a demo").

- **Any price, at any time.** The founder's $300 to $600 per agent a month is the operator's reading (item 7), recorded

  number, not Lemma's.
- **A share of runs.** [LYC]'s 40 is a fall in "performance", not a share of failing runs; the RATE reading and its low
  end of 10 are the author's (header).
- **A buyer title in practice, the approvers and the purchase steps.** Only the launch ask names the buyer; the CEO and
  security lead, the three Purchase friction items and the trial step are the author's.
- **An engineer's hour.** [BLS]'s software developers' median stands in; a RATE cost does not use it.
- **The daily rhythm at launch.** The launch says "continuously"; the morning-check quote is today's site.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person engineer accounts from the launch era.** None found; the customer quotes on
  [SITE] are vendor-curated and later than launch.

screens.why3: I know exactly what my engineers do today (dig through logs, collect failing examples, hand-tweak prompts) and what Lemma replaces, so I can answer from my own launch claims.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with one escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' fits a founder who does not want to test the advantage.
screens.why5: I typed two benefits, but Keel's belief keeps only 'the fix found in minutes, not days' and silently drops 'no hand-tuning prompts against failing examples', which is the 90% cut in manual prompt iteration I lead with.
screens.instead: Keep both benefits in the belief: 'For most, their last failure would have gone better with it: the fix found in minutes, not days, without hand-tuning prompts against failing examples.'

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today's way, this is where I check Keel's list of benefits before it goes to strangers, so it obviously belongs here.
screens.why2: "Hand-tuning prompts against failing examples" and "the fix found in minutes, not days" are exactly how an engineer running an agent in production talks about this work.
screens.why3: Every engineer I'm targeting has had a production failure and remembers how long the fix took and how much prompt-tweaking it needed.
screens.why4: Both rows are mine and distinct, but the benefit my whole launch leads with is missing: failures caught in live traffic before customers find them.
screens.why5: The rows keep my launch claims, "resolve production drifts in minutes instead of days" and the cut in manual prompt iteration; "No hand-tuning" rounds my 90% up to all, which I can live with.
screens.instead: Rows: The fix found in minutes, not days / Failures caught before customers report them / Far less hand-tuning of prompts against failing examples

screens.why1: After what it fits and what it does better, asking what my engineers must do to start is the obvious next step in Step 3.
screens.why2: 'Setup, extra steps or learning' is plain to me as a founder of a dev tool, and the 25-word limit is clear.
screens.why3: I know exactly what onboarding asks of a team: instrument the agent with our tracing, then review the PRs we open.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a free-text answer I might not want tested.
screens.why5: I typed two steps, but the belief keeps only 'review and merge the prompt changes it opens'. That is ongoing use, not setup, and it drops 'add its tracing to the agent's code', the real first step.
screens.instead: What will they have to do to start using it? (Belief kept as: Most would add its tracing to their agent's code and review and merge the prompt changes it opens.)

screens.why1: After I said what they'll have to do to start, checking Keel's list of those steps and picking one to test is the obvious next screen.
screens.why2: Prompt changes, merge, tracing and live traffic are everyday words to an engineer running an agent in production, and each row reads on first pass.
screens.why3: Adding an SDK's tracing, wiring it to prod traffic and reviewing a PR are things these engineers do with their own hands every week.
screens.why4: 'Add its tracing to the agent's code' and 'Connect it to the live agent's traffic' are the same onboarding step seen twice, since the tracing is how it sees live traffic, so one adoption cost is missing: letting it read the prompts in our repo and open PRs there.
screens.why5: The two steps I named, reviewing and merging the PRs it opens and adding its tracing, are kept word for word, and the belief tests the PR step I care about.
screens.instead: What they'll have to do: Add its tracing to the agent's code / Review and merge the prompt changes it opens / Give it access to the repo where prompts live

screens.why1: Right after I named what engineers must do to start, asking which of those efforts is most likely to stop them is the obvious next step before the test is set.
screens.why2: Prompt changes, merge, tracing and traffic are everyday words to me and to the engineers I sell to, and the question reads on first pass.
screens.why3: I know which step my users balk at: letting a machine open PRs against prompts they own is the real fear, so I can pick without guessing.
screens.why4: My two efforts are there in my words, but the third, 'Connect it to the live agent's traffic', is really the same act as adding our tracing to the agent's code (the tracing is how we see live traffic), so two options overlap.
screens.why5: The belief and test, 'Most would review and merge the prompt changes it opens', is exactly the adoption step I typed and meant to test.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? — Review and merge the prompt changes it opens / Add its tracing to the agent's code / Let its traces leave the company (security review)

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious moment to decide whether to collect emails from people who want to try it, and my launch is built on booking demos with exactly those people.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is plain to a founder selling dev tooling, and the hint quotes the exact line respondents will see, so I know what I'm switching on.
screens.why3: Whether I want design partners from this study is my own call; I'm actively asking for teams to work with us.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole decision here, and both chips are distinct and say what they do.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks; the respondent line is generic, though 'try this for real' is vaguer than my actual next step of connecting one agent's traces for a trial.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Yes: ask them to leave an email to connect one agent's traces for a trial / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs in the last step before the link goes out, right after deciding on a pilot.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint says the questions are asked 'on video' while the choice is between voices you only 'hear', so I'd re-read to work out whether I'm picking a face, a voice or both, and the credits line adds a second read.
screens.why3: I can answer it from my own taste after five seconds of each sample, with no guessing about anyone else's job.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers with a sample each and a preselected default cover the choice, and the hint says typing or tapping is always possible, so no text-only escape is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps my respondents as 'AI engineers' and shows nothing of Lemma's product or my buyer roles to the people who will answer.
screens.instead: Who should ask AI engineers your questions? (Each interviewer appears on video and reads every question aloud; the question is also on screen to read and answer by typing or tapping.) Options: Daphne ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s

screens.why1: Choosing how engineers will answer belongs right after choosing who asks them and just before sending, so I see why it is asked here.
screens.why2: The choice itself is clear, but "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" and the line about catching spoken answers 9 in 10 times where it is loud are status and accuracy notes I have to read twice to see why they matter to me.
screens.why3: I know my engineers are at their desks and would rather tap through than talk to a video, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: AI interviewer, read and tap, and let them choose cover the real options without overlap, and each says when it will be ready.
screens.why5: It names my respondents as AI engineers, exactly as I typed them, and nothing of my product leaks into the formats.
screens.instead: How should AI engineers answer? — Read and tap (ready now) / Talk to Daphne, an AI interviewer on video (ready in a few minutes) / Let them pick when they open the link

screens.why1: Once I've picked who asks and how engineers answer, the obvious next question is who receives the link, and it is the last step before I send.
screens.why2: Mostly plain to me, but "the Contacts page" names a Keel page I haven't used in this flow, so the middle option takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know who I'd send this to: engineers I've worked with from Tandem and Chipstack, YC batchmates, or an AI-engineering Slack I could post in.
screens.why4: The three routes (named people, a list Keel found, one open link in a community) cover how I'd reach engineers, they don't overlap, and none is silly.
screens.why5: My pick, people I know by name, is kept as typed, and nothing about Lemma or my roles shows through to an engineer.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (one link each) / A list Keel found for me (Keel makes a link for each; you send them) / A group I'm already in, like a Slack or Discord (one open link; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated with '4 answered' beside it, but the bar it misses, 5 needed, sits only on the cards, and the line names Compatibility alone when all three cards are short.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart, only the tally; '3 too few · 7 people answered' next to cards that each say '4 answered' made me look twice to work out where the other 3 went.
screens.why_b3: All three dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked, word for word, though the solution paragraph above them is garbled: it has the engineer watching traffic and alerting 'you'.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: not how many more engineers to reach, nor whether to resend the study to the ones who did not count.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing it cannot carry: every card says too few, with n and the needed count shown.
screens.instead: None of your three solution beliefs can be called yet: 4 of the 7 engineers who answered were counted on each, and 5 are needed. Send the study to at least one more engineer whose agent is live to get a verdict, and see why 3 were not counted.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside its number, but the header says '4 answered' while the count line says '5 answered · 4 counted', so the deciding number is mislabelled until the So line says '4 counted, 5 needed'.
screens.why_b2: It counts better against same over 4 people, but the doubled '3 3' and the bar given as both '3 of 4' and 'no more than 1 in 3 say no difference or worse' take a second look to see that 1 of 4 against clears it.
screens.why_b3: The card's name and my belief are word for word what I checked: Relative advantage, the fix found in minutes, not days.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say that 3 of the 4 counted already sit inside my bar, or that one more counted answer, such as Kwabena's, would settle it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', the answer is flagged as a hypothetical, and nothing claims the belief held.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 5 needed were counted (Kwabena's answer was a guess). So far it leans your way, 3 'a lot better' and 1 'no difference', within your bar, so get one more clear answer to make the call.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside "4 answered · 5 needed to call it", and the So line repeats the same 4-of-5 shortfall, so I know where I stand and why.
screens.why_b2: Four answers are counted, 2 plain yes and 2 conditional yes against 0 no, the bar is at 3 of 4, and the strip shows 4 for, 1 ghost and the marker at 3, all readable at once.
screens.why_b3: The title "Adoption friction" and the line "Most would review and merge the prompt changes it opens" are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic: it doesn't tell me that one more counted answer decides it, or that half my yeses depend on the fix being clearly worth it, which is what I'd actually go test.
screens.why_b5: The header says "4 answered" while the count line says "5 answered · 4 counted", which muddles my n even though nothing claims strength ("a lean, not a call" is honest).
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted would merge Lemma's prompt PRs, but 2 only if it's clearly worth it; one more counted answer decides it, so show the fix's value up front in the trial.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside "4 answered · 5 needed to call it", so I know there is no verdict yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Relative advantage and the belief line is word for word the one I checked: the fix found in minutes, not days.
screens.why_b4: "5 needed" hints that I need one more answer, but the screen never says to get one, or what Aisha's eval-suite answer means for my pitch to teams that already run evals.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the low count is named as too few, and the single quote is shown as one person (1 against, 1 asked), not as a trend.
screens.why_b6: Aisha's answer adds something I never typed: a team's own eval suite already catches regressions before they ship, so for them the real slips are shipping on time and latency, not drift.

screens.why1: As the opening gate it's obvious why it's asked: it checks whether I've had a production failure recently enough to tell a fresh story about.
screens.why2: 'Start failing' trips me up, because our agent fails a little every day and nothing 'started', and 'real inputs' isn't how I'd say it; I'd say customer traffic or something we never tested.
screens.why3: Yes, I watch our traces and incident channel every day, so I know whether it broke on something new this week.
screens.why4: Yes and No are fine, but a gate shouldn't carry escape chips at all, and 'I'd rather not say' is a chip that isn't supposed to exist; 'I can't recall one particular failure' is a sentence that overlaps with No.
screens.why5: Dropping 'that never came up in testing' leaves just 'failing', so any routine bad tool call or timeout counts as a yes, which isn't the situation the founder means.
screens.why6: Heard once, it's short, it's one question, and 'Yes or no' closes it cleanly.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did your agent fail on a customer request you'd never tested for? Yes / No (no escape).

screens.why1: Right after I said my agent broke on real inputs this week, showing me an idea for catching and fixing that is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Live traffic, agent chain, eval sets, tracing and drift alerts are all my everyday words, but 'Lemma, a prompt pull request' made me stop, because a pull request is what the tool opens, not what the tool is.
screens.why3: I triage failing traces, tweak prompts and push PRs myself, so I can judge this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options.
screens.why5: The idea comes through, but the first line names an output instead of saying what it is, and the belief re-lists the how ('exact cause in the agent chain', 'improved prompt in the pull request') instead of pointing back to it.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is eight sentences in a row with a feature list tacked on the end, and 'a prompt pull request' does not land by ear, though nothing in it is unsayable.
screens.instead: Imagine Lemma, a tool that catches your agent's failures in production and proposes a prompt fix as a pull request. It watches live traffic, finds which step in the agent chain caused a failure and alerts you; one click tests a better prompt and opens a pull request with it, alongside your evals, traces and drift alerts. The people building it believe this would get you from a failure to a fix much faster.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, it makes sense to ask whether I already had every production run traced, since a prompt PR tool would need those traces to work from.
screens.why2: 'Traced' and 'run of the agent' are how we talk about LangSmith or Langfuse spans every day, and 'your last failure' points back to the screen-one incident clearly enough.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether tracing was on for all our prod traffic when the agent broke, so I can answer from what we actually had.
screens.why4: 'Yes, with some steps' doesn't fit a past fact like 'did you already have it traced'; the real middle answer is 'only some runs' or 'sampled', and that's missing.
screens.why5: The question tests one thing the idea depends on, existing traces, without leaking how Lemma works beyond the card shown on purpose.
screens.why6: It's short and one question, with three options I can hold on one hearing and a single escape said last.

screens.why1: After asking whether Lemma would have helped my last failure, it makes sense to ask whether I'd do the one thing it needs from me, which is reviewing its PRs.
screens.why2: Review and merge are what I do with PRs every day, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I already review and merge prompt changes from teammates, so I know whether I'd take them from a tool.
screens.why4: The four steps run from yes to no without overlapping, and the conditional yes is the honest middle for most of us; only a 'yes, but I'd edit them first' is missing, and the conditional yes mostly covers that.
screens.why5: 'Prompt changes it opens' is slightly off, since a tool opens pull requests rather than changes, and the card calling Lemma 'a prompt pull request' makes the product sound like a single PR instead of something that writes them.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is short and one question, with four short options I can hold and a clean escape.
screens.instead: To use Lemma, you'd review and merge the prompt pull requests it opens. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Yes, after editing them · Yes, if it was clearly worth it · No · (I can't tell)
